About: the stellar thermostat: an ideal-gas core against a degenerate core after a surge of nuclear energy

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the helium core on the dark interior of the star, its colour set by its temperature on a fixed key from 0.9 to 1.5 × 108 K, a central glow whose brightness follows log10(Lnuc/L) on a fixed scale from −2 to 8, arrows for the steady loss L and a dashed circle at the starting radius R0. Right: T against t, 0 to 1.5 τ, with the current run bright and the three previous runs fainter.
Controls
Core (ideal gas or degenerate), the temperature exponent ζ of the reaction rate (4, 20 or 40) and the surge as a percentage of the thermal energy E0; changing any of them returns the core to T0 with the clock at zero. ⚡ Release surge releases the extra energy and starts the clock; ⏮ Rewind returns the core to T0 with the clock at zero.
Measured
t in units of τ = E0/L, T in units of 108 K (T0 = 1 × 108 K), Lnuc/L and its log10 and R/R0, all from the engine's exact solution t(θ); the clock runs at 0.1 τ per second and holds where a degenerate run stops at 1.5 T0. All of these are in the Readouts panel of the sidebar.
Model
The burning rate is Lnuc = L(T/T0)ζ, with ζ ≈ 4 for the pp chain, 20 for the CNO cycle and 40 for triple-alpha. The ideal-gas core is assumed to stay in virial equilibrium (Etot = −Eth, so its heat capacity is negative), readjusting at once because its dynamical time is far shorter than τ. The degenerate core keeps its radius and has a positive heat capacity. Stopping at 1.5 T0, where the thermal pressure is taken to overcome degeneracy, is a choice of the model; in a real helium flash the core then expands and the runaway ends.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The moment after the surge

Choose the ideal-gas core, set ζ to 40 and the surge to 5%. The core starts at T0 with the clock at zero. Before pressing ⚡ Release surge, predict what the temperature of the core does in the moment after the extra energy is released. Then press it and watch the temperature readout and the T–t plot.

2 · What follows the dip

Keep the settings of question 1; the core is back at T0. Before pressing ⚡ Release surge, predict what happens to the core after the dip in temperature. Then press it and watch the glow, the radius readout and the T–t plot until the clock reaches 1.5τ.

3 · A degenerate core

Choose the degenerate core and keep ζ at 40 and the surge at 5%; the core is back at T0. Before pressing ⚡ Release surge, predict what the temperature of this core does after the surge. Then press it and watch the temperature and Lnuc/L.

4 · The smallest surge

Keep the degenerate core and ζ = 40, and set the surge to 1%, the smallest it can be. Before pressing ⚡ Release surge, predict what happens this time.

5 · Burning rate at the end

Keep the degenerate core and set the surge to 5%. You will run it once with ζ = 4 and once with ζ = 40, and read Lnuc/L when the simulation stops at 1.5T0. Before you do, predict the two readings.

6 · Two recoveries compared

Choose the ideal-gas core and keep the surge at 5%. You will run it once with ζ = 4 and once with ζ = 40 and compare the two traces in the T–t plot. Before you do, predict how the two recoveries to T0 compare.

7 · What you found

An ideal-gas core has a negative heat capacity, so a burst of energy makes it expand and cool; the burning slows and the core returns to T0 over a time τ/ζ. That is the stellar thermostat. A degenerate core does not expand, so the same burst heats it, speeds the burning and runs away, with no threshold; for triple-alpha burning (ζ ≈ 40) this is the helium flash. The model assumes the ideal-gas core readjusts to equilibrium at once, and it ends the runaway at 1.5T0, where degeneracy is taken to be lifted.

Two Cores and a Burst of Energy

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Deep in a red giant, a helium core burns at about 108 K. This sim gives such a core a sudden surge of extra nuclear energy and follows what happens next, for two kinds of core. It shows the core's colour and size, its burning rate as a glow, and a plot of temperature against time.

What you'll learn

  • How a stellar core responds when it gains energy suddenly.
  • What the exponent ζ of the burning rate controls.
  • What this model leaves out.
The opening state, sketched: the core at its starting radius R₀, the steady loss L, and the temperature plot with its dashed line at T₀.

What's on screen

  • The core, with its radius R drawn against the dashed circle of the starting radius R₀. Its colour is the temperature on a fixed key from 0.9 to 1.5 × 108 K, and arrows leave it at the steady loss L.
  • The glow at the centre grows brighter with log10(Lnuc/L), on a fixed scale from −2 to 8.
  • The plot of T against t, from 0 to 1.5 τ. The current run is bright, the three before it fainter, and T₀ is dashed.
  • Readouts: the time t since the surge, T, R/R₀, Lnuc/L and its logarithm.
See itLook at the core before any surge is released. Watch for: Temperature T reading 1.0000 × 10⁸ K, R/R₀ reading 1.0000 and Lnuc/L reading 1.000, with the clock at 0.000 τ.

03

Extra energy cools an ideal-gas core: Etot = −Eth

For a core of ideal gas the virial theorem of Section 4.2 holds (notes 4.7). Its total energy is therefore minus its thermal energy:

Notes, Section 4.7. Eth is the thermal energy and Egrav the gravitational potential energy.

A surge raises Etot, so Eth falls by the same amount and the core cools. A surge of a fraction s of E0 gives the first equation below. Since Egrav = −2Eth, the core also expands.

The sim's ideal-gas core, taken to be in its new equilibrium at once. No rise comes first.
A 5 % surge in the ideal-gas core. Energies are in units of E0, and dashed outlines show the bars before the surge.

A 5 % surge gives T = 0.9500 T₀ and R = 1.0526 R₀. A 10 % surge gives 0.9000 and 1.1111.

surge

This slider moves the sim's surge too, which returns the core to T₀.

Key idea. An ideal-gas core has a negative heat capacity. Energy added to it makes it expand and cool.
See itRelease a 5 % surge in the ideal-gas core at ζ = 40, and stop at the moment of release. Watch for: Temperature T reading 0.9500 × 10⁸ K, R/R₀ reading 1.0526, and Lnuc/L reading 0.129.
04

A cool core heats back to T₀ over a time of order τ/ζ

The burning power is Lnuc = L (T/T₀)ζ, with ζ ≈ 4 for the pp chain, ≈ 20 for the CNO cycle and ≈ 40 for triple-alpha burning (notes 4.4).

At T₀ the burning exactly balances the loss L.

Below T₀ the burning falls short of the loss: at 0.9500 T₀ and ζ = 40, Lnuc/L is 0.129. The core loses energy, and an ideal gas that loses energy contracts and heats. With Eth proportional to T the energy balance becomes the following, with t in units of τ:

The sim's equation for the ideal-gas core. The time unit is τ = E0/L.
The recovery after a 5 % surge, from the sim's solution. T climbs to T₀ and never overshoots it.

At ζ = 40 the temperature reaches 0.9699 at 0.025 τ and 0.9973 at 0.1 τ. Near T₀ a small departure dies away as e−ζt/τ, over a time τ/ζ. T comes within 0.0005 of T₀ after 0.143 τ at ζ = 40, and after 1.17 τ at ζ = 4.

Key idea. Burning that rises with temperature and a core that cools when it gains energy make a thermostat. A steeper ζ holds T₀ more tightly.
See itRelease the same surge and stop the clock at 0.1 τ. Watch for: Temperature T back at 0.9973 × 10⁸ K, R/R₀ at 1.0027, and the bright trace nearly level with the dashed T₀ line.
05

A degenerate core heats and runs away, with no threshold

In a degenerate core the pressure hardly depends on temperature, so the core does not expand, and the energy released only raises the temperature (notes 4.7). The surge adds directly: T = (1 + s) T₀ and R stays R₀. Above T₀ the burning exceeds the loss, so the core heats further.

The sim's equation for the degenerate core, in units of τ. The sim stops it at θ = 1.5.

A 5 % surge at ζ = 40 starts at 1.0500 T₀ with Lnuc/L = 7.040 and reaches 1.5 T₀ after only 0.00412 τ. On the plot it looks like a jump. There is no threshold, since any T above T₀ makes θζ exceed 1. A 1 % surge still runs away, after 0.0287 τ.

A degenerate core after a 5 % surge, from the sim's solution. Time is on a logarithmic axis.
Key idea. The same surge heats a degenerate core, and heat speeds the burning, which heats it more. Nothing stops the runaway but the model's limit.
See itChoose the degenerate core at ζ = 40 and release a 5 % surge. Watch for: T stopping at 1.5000 × 10⁸ K after 0.00412 τ, with Lnuc/L reading 1.11 × 10⁷ and R/R₀ staying 1.0000.
See itNow set the surge to 1 %, the smallest. Watch for: the run still ending at 1.5000 × 10⁸ K, after 0.0287 τ, with Lnuc/L starting at only 1.489.
06

The exponent sets the pace: τ/ζ for the thermostat, 1.5ζ at the stop

In the ideal-gas core a steeper ζ means a faster return, over τ/ζ. In the degenerate core a steeper ζ means a faster and higher runaway. At the stop, T = 1.5 T₀, so Lnuc/L = 1.5ζ whatever the surge. The table is for a 5 % surge.

ζReactionIdeal core: τ/ζDegenerate core: time to 1.5 T₀Lnuc/L at 1.5 T₀
4pp chain0.250 τ0.440 τ5.063
20CNO cycle0.0500 τ0.0260 τ3.33 × 103
40triple-alpha0.0250 τ0.00412 τ1.11 × 107

The surge sets the starting point and the time to run away, not the end. At ζ = 40 the runaway takes 0.0287 τ for a 1 % surge and 0.00063 τ for a 10 % surge, and both end at 1.11 × 107.

See itChoose the degenerate core at ζ = 4 and release a 5 % surge. Watch for: T stopping at 1.5000 × 10⁸ K after 0.440 τ, with Lnuc/L reading 5.063, where ζ = 40 reached 1.11 × 10⁷.
07

Where it matters

  • Steady burning. In a core of ideal gas the burning of a nuclear fuel regulates itself (notes 4.7). A brief excess of energy makes the core expand and cool, and the reaction rate falls back.
  • The helium flash. At the tip of the red-giant branch the core is about 0.45 M⊙ and degenerate, with its centre near 108 K. Helium ignites, and with ζ ≈ 40 the burning runs away. For a few seconds the rate may reach 1011 L⊙. The energy goes into expanding the core, so the flash cannot be seen from outside.
  • The end of the flash. The runaway stops when the electrons' thermal pressure again exceeds their degeneracy pressure. The core then expands and burns helium steadily. The sim ends its run at 1.5 T₀ in place of that expansion.
Go deeper: where ζ comes from and what the model assumes
  • The triple-alpha rate goes as T−3 e−Q3α/kBT (4.72), so near a temperature T it goes as Tζ with ζ = Q3α/kBT − 3, about 40 at 108 K.
  • The sim offers ζ = 4, 20 and 40 at the same T₀ = 108 K to compare the exponents. In nature the pp and CNO values belong to temperatures near the Sun's centre.
  • The ideal-gas core is assumed to readjust at once, since its dynamical time is far shorter than τ. The degenerate core is assumed to keep its radius, and the stop at 1.5 T₀ is the model's choice.
08

Summary

In one line. This sim follows a stellar core after a sudden surge of nuclear energy, for two kinds of core and three values of the exponent ζ of the burning rate.

Key points

  • Ideal-gas core: Etot = −Eth, so a surge s gives T = (1 − s) T₀ and R = R₀/(1 − s). The core returns to T₀ over a time of order τ/ζ.
  • Degenerate core: no expansion, so T = (1 + s) T₀, and any s runs away. The sim stops it at 1.5 T₀, where Lnuc/L = 1.5ζ.
  • The runaway at the triple-alpha exponent ζ ≈ 40 is the helium flash.

Common mix-ups

  • "Extra energy makes the core hotter." In an ideal gas a 5 % surge drops T/T₀ to 0.9500.
  • "A 1 % surge is too small to run away." In a degenerate core any rise above T₀ runs away, here after 0.0287 τ.

Things to try on your own

  • Release a 10 % surge in the ideal-gas core and compare T and R/R₀ with 1 − s and 1/(1 − s).
  • Run the degenerate core at ζ = 40 with the surge at 1, 5 and 10 %, and note each time to reach 1.5 T₀.
